name: Marrakech
tagline: The Red City of storytellers, souks and sunset squares.
scene: Jemaa el-Fna Square and the Koutoubia area
description: Marrakech is one of Morocco’s most energetic cities. Its medina mixes traditional souks, riads, gardens, storytellers, food stalls and historic monuments. The visual focuses on the atmosphere of Jemaa el-Fna with the Koutoubia minaret nearby: the heart of the old city at sunset.
experience: Start near Jemaa el-Fna in the late afternoon, walk through the souks, then enjoy a rooftop view as the square becomes full of music, food smoke and street performances.
culture: Marrakech is a meeting point between Amazigh, Arab-Andalusian and Saharan influences. Its culture is visible in the rhythm of Jemaa el-Fna: storytellers, musicians, orange-juice stalls, henna artists, spice sellers and rooftop cafés that turn the square into a living open-air theater.
heritage: The city is strongly linked to the Almoravid and Saadian periods, with landmarks such as the Koutoubia Mosque exterior, Bahia Palace, Saadian Tombs and traditional riads inside the medina.
localFood: Try tanjia marrakchia, slow-cooked meat traditionally prepared in clay pots, plus harira soup, dates, msemen and fresh mint tea.
craft: Marrakech is famous for leather goods, lanterns, carpets, spices, carved wood, metalwork and colorful souk craftsmanship.
visitTip: The best atmosphere around Jemaa el-Fna starts in the late afternoon and continues after sunset. For the map marker, use Jemaa el-Fna because that is the scene shown in the hero image.

name: Casablanca
scene: Hassan II Mosque on the Atlantic Ocean
description: Casablanca is Morocco’s economic capital and one of its most contemporary cities. The image highlights the Hassan II Mosque, a monumental seaside landmark where Moroccan craftsmanship, zellige details and ocean scenery meet.
experience: Visit the Hassan II Mosque area, walk along the Atlantic promenade, then discover the contrast between modern boulevards and the traditional Habous district.
culture: Casablanca represents modern Morocco: business, ocean life, cafés, Art Deco buildings and a younger urban energy. The culture here is less medina-centered than Fes or Marrakech, but it shows how Morocco connects tradition with contemporary city life.
heritage: The Hassan II Mosque is the main cultural landmark in the image. It combines monumental scale with Moroccan craftsmanship: carved plaster, zellige, cedarwood and a dramatic Atlantic setting.
localFood: Casablanca is excellent for seafood, grilled fish, Moroccan salads and modern café culture along the Corniche.
craft: Look for traditional items in the Habous Quarter, where arches, bookshops, pastry shops and artisan stores create a calmer historical district.
visitTip: Place the marker on Hassan II Mosque, not just Casablanca center, because the photo is specifically about the mosque by the Atlantic.

name: Fes
tagline: A living medieval medina of knowledge and craft.
description: Fes is the spiritual and intellectual capital of Morocco, famous for Fes el-Bali, madrasas, artisans and narrow alleys. The image shows the Chouara Tannery, one of the most recognizable traditional craft sites in the city.
experience: Enter through Bab Boujloud, follow the medina lanes with a guide, then visit a tannery terrace to understand the leather-making tradition that has shaped Fes for centuries.
culture: Fes is one of Morocco’s deepest cultural capitals. Its medina is a world of craftsmen, Quranic schools, narrow alleys, fountains, mosques, markets and family workshops where many skills are passed from generation to generation.
heritage: The image shows the Chouara Tannery, a famous leather-production site in Fes el-Bali. The city is also associated with Al Quaraouiyine, madrasas, Andalusian neighborhoods and traditional medina urbanism.
localFood: Fassi cuisine is refined and often includes sweet-savory combinations, pastilla, slow-cooked meat, olives, preserved lemon and pastries.
craft: Fes is known for leather, zellige tilework, brassware, embroidery, carved wood and ceramic pottery.
visitTip: Use a guide inside the medina and mark Chouara Tannery for this image, because the photo shows the tannery vats rather than a general Fes skyline.

name: Chefchaouen
tagline: The blue mountain medina of the Rif.
scene: Blue-painted streets of the old medina
description: Chefchaouen is known for its calm blue-painted streets, mountain backdrop and relaxed atmosphere. The visual focuses on the narrow medina stairways, blue walls, doors and potted plants that make the city instantly recognizable.
experience: Spend time walking slowly through the blue alleys, stop for tea in the main square, then climb toward the Spanish Mosque viewpoint for sunset over the medina.
culture: Chefchaouen is calm, artistic and mountain-rooted. Its blue medina is connected to local identity, hospitality, small guesthouses, slow walking, handmade textiles and the Rif Mountains around it.
heritage: The old medina developed with Andalusian and Amazigh influences. Its white-and-blue walls, small squares, doors, stairs and plants create one of Morocco’s most recognizable urban atmospheres.
localFood: Try mountain goat cheese, olive oil, traditional bread, tajines and mint tea in the main square.
craft: Local shops often sell woven blankets, wool garments, leather items, ceramics and small painted souvenirs inspired by the blue city.
visitTip: For the map, mark the old medina/Outa el Hammam area because the photo is about the blue streets, not the modern town outside the medina.

name: Merzouga
tagline: Gateway to the golden dunes of Erg Chebbi.
description: Merzouga is the classic starting point for the Moroccan Sahara. The image represents the Erg Chebbi dunes, camel caravans, warm desert light and the feeling of silence that makes this part of Morocco unforgettable.
experience: Arrive before sunset, ride or walk into the dunes, sleep in a desert camp, then wake early for sunrise when the sand changes color from gold to rose.
culture: Merzouga is shaped by Saharan life, desert hospitality, nomadic traditions and the music of nearby Khamlia. The experience is about silence, dunes, stars, camel paths and small communities living close to the desert environment.
heritage: The image represents Erg Chebbi, the large dune field beside Merzouga. It is one of the most iconic Sahara landscapes in Morocco and an important stop on desert routes.
localFood: Expect tajine, bread baked in sand or clay ovens in some experiences, dates, tea and simple camp dinners under the stars.
craft: Desert-region crafts include woven textiles, scarves, jewelry, leather bags and Amazigh-inspired patterns.
visitTip: The correct marker is Erg Chebbi dunes near Merzouga. Sunset and sunrise are the strongest moments for photography.

name: Essaouira
tagline: Atlantic wind, blue boats and fortified walls.
scene: Essaouira fishing port and Skala walls
description: Essaouira combines ocean air, Portuguese-influenced fortifications, white-and-blue architecture and a famous working fishing port. The visual focuses on the blue boats and the historic coastal ramparts.
experience: Walk around the port in the morning, explore the medina’s artisan shops, then enjoy seafood near the harbor before sunset along the ramparts.
culture: Essaouira has a coastal identity: fishing boats, seagulls, ramparts, wind, music festivals and a relaxed medina. It mixes Amazigh, Arab, Jewish, Portuguese and Atlantic influences.
heritage: The photo shows the working fishing port and fortified walls. Essaouira is known for Skala de la Ville, sea-facing bastions, blue boats and a UNESCO-listed medina plan.
localFood: Fresh grilled fish and seafood are central. You can also find Moroccan salads, sardines, calamari, mint tea and almond pastries.
craft: Essaouira is famous for thuya woodwork, small galleries, silver jewelry, textiles and artisan workshops inside the medina.
visitTip: Mark Essaouira Port/Skala area because the image shows blue boats and fortifications beside the water.

name: Rabat
tagline: A calm capital where history meets the Atlantic.
description: Rabat is Morocco’s administrative capital, elegant and organized but still rich in heritage. The image shows the Hassan Tower site, one of the city’s main symbols, surrounded by columns, gardens and historic architecture.
experience: Begin with Hassan Tower and the mausoleum, continue to the Kasbah of the Udayas, then end the day near the Bouregreg river or the Atlantic coast.
culture: Rabat feels calmer and more organized than many Moroccan cities. As the capital, it combines administration, royal history, coastal neighborhoods, gardens and a strong cultural-institutional presence.
heritage: The Hassan Tower site, shown in the image, is one of Rabat’s key symbols. The site includes the unfinished minaret, historic columns and the nearby Mausoleum of Mohammed V.
localFood: Rabat offers classic Moroccan cuisine, seafood, pastries and relaxed cafés near the river and the old city.
craft: The medina and nearby areas include carpets, leather goods, pottery, embroidery and traditional clothing.
visitTip: Use Hassan Tower as the map marker because the photo is a landmark scene of the tower and surrounding historical plaza.

name: Tangier
tagline: The northern gateway between Africa and Europe.
scene: Tangier Kasbah and old medina overlooking the bay
description: Tangier sits at the meeting point of the Atlantic and Mediterranean worlds. The image represents the white medina and coastal view from the Kasbah area, showing the city’s bright northern character and sea-facing identity.
experience: Explore the Kasbah and medina lanes, look toward the bay from the upper city, then continue to Cap Spartel where the Atlantic and Mediterranean routes meet.
culture: Tangier has always been a city of crossing: Africa and Europe, Atlantic and Mediterranean, Arabic, Amazigh, Spanish and French influences. Its culture feels international while still deeply Moroccan.
heritage: The photo represents the Kasbah/old medina overlook, with white buildings, blue details and sea views. Tangier’s history is tied to ports, diplomacy, writers, cafés and strategic geography.
localFood: Seafood, fish tajine, fresh bread, olives, tea and northern Moroccan pastries are common highlights.
craft: The medina offers textiles, leather, brass lamps, pottery and northern-style souvenirs.
visitTip: Mark the Kasbah Museum / upper medina area for this image because that is where the white city and bay views are best represented.

name: Aït Ben Haddou
tagline: An earthen ksar on the old caravan route.
scene: Ksar of Aït Ben Haddou beside the Ounila Valley
description: Aït Ben Haddou is a fortified earthen village near Ouarzazate and one of Morocco’s most famous desert-route heritage sites. The image focuses on the clay architecture, palm greenery and rocky landscape that define the ksar.
experience: Cross toward the ksar, climb through the narrow passages to the upper viewpoint, and take time to appreciate the mud-brick construction and valley landscape.
mapsQuery: Ksar of Ait Ben Haddou Morocco
culture: Aït Ben Haddou represents the culture of southern Morocco: earthen architecture, caravan routes, Amazigh heritage, desert-edge villages and valley agriculture. The ksar shows how communities adapted to climate and trade routes.
heritage: The image shows the fortified ksar made of mud brick and clay. It is one of Morocco’s most famous UNESCO heritage scenes and is connected to the old route between the Sahara and Marrakech.
localFood: Typical local meals include tajines, couscous, dates, bread, olives and tea served in family guesthouses or roadside cafés.
craft: Look for Amazigh carpets, woven textiles, clay architecture details, local paintings and desert-route souvenirs.
visitTip: The correct marker is the Ksar of Aït Ben Haddou itself, not the center of Ouarzazate.
